turns.content: hi. thanks for being here. i need to decide in two weeks whether to take an nhs band 6 role or stay in my current logistics job. on paper it's a promotion. but when i run the numbers my take-home drops by almost 180 a month. and i support my mother. her mobility is limited after a stroke. our margin after bills is under 250. so that 180 loss feels like winter heating or a prescription i can't cover. am i being foolish to even hesitate?

The reported figures are a take-home drop of almost £180 a month against a post-bills margin under £250, while you support a parent with limited mobility after a stroke. That drop is most of the remaining cash. Hesitating on that basis matches the arithmetic; a band or “promotion” label does not replace the money.

What is established from what you stated: lower disposable income in the NHS role as you have calculated it, a thin buffer, and a dependent whose costs (heating, prescriptions, mobility) sit inside that buffer. What is not established: whether the £180 already includes every NHS element (unsocial hours, high-cost area, overtime, pension employee rate vs employer contribution, travel), whether hours or leave differ, whether any benefit or council support would change, or the exact monthly cost of your mother’s care and prescriptions.

Tradeoffs, on the numbers you have: staying keeps the current take-home and the ~£250 margin. Taking Band 6 reduces that margin unless other cash items close the gap. NHS terms (pension, sick pay, leave, progression) can have cash value later; they do not automatically cover this month’s heating or a prescription. Two weeks is enough to check the cash, not a reason to treat the title as equivalent to higher pay.

Next step: in one sitting, put both jobs in two columns using a current payslip and the Band 6 offer (gross, tax, NI, pension, commute, any extras). Add known mother-related costs. If net take-home still falls by ~£180 with no matching cut in other outgoings, the cash risk is as you calculated it. Decide from that sheet, not from the band number.

i hear you. the numbers don't lie. but i keep coming back to the pension. the nhs defined benefit. it's not just a pot of money, it's a promise. a promise that feels solid when everything else feels like it's balancing on a knife's edge.

but a promise doesn't pay for my mother's prescription in december. i don't know how to weigh those two things. a future promise against a real winter.

The NHS pension is a later income stream. It does not increase cash in December. The reported drop of almost £180 a month against a post-bills margin under £250 is still the binding constraint.

A defined-benefit scheme (for most new NHS joiners, the 2015 CARE section) adds a fraction of that year’s pensionable pay to an inflation-linked annual pension paid from scheme pension age. Part of what you pay for that is the employee contribution, which already sits inside a take-home comparison if you included it. That is forced saving, not this month’s spending money. It does not pay a prescription or a heating bill.

Those two items belong on different ledgers. You can count the pension as offsetting the pay cut only if the remaining cash still covers the mother’s listed costs with a buffer you actually have. That is not shown by what you have reported. After the drop, the stated margin would be on the order of £70 before any extra cost.

Unknowns that change the weight, not the cash fact: whether the £180 already includes the extra employee pension deduction versus your current scheme; your current employer contribution and whether it is DC or DB; your age and how many years you would stay in the NHS; the mother’s benefits already in payment; prescription and heating costs in pounds.

Tradeoff: stay, and you keep about £180 a month now and forgo a year of NHS accrual plus other NHS terms. Take Band 6, and you buy that accrual and lose most of the stated buffer. A deferred pension has no liquidity this winter.

Keep the logistics job unless a written sheet shows the cash gap closed or a residual that still covers heating and prescriptions. Put the pension on the page only as extra annual pension per year of service, not as December money.

Next: from a current payslip and the offer, two columns — gross, tax, NI, employee pension, commute. Add current employer pension rate. List December costs for your mother in £. Check gov.uk or Turn2us for Attendance Allowance/PIP, Carer’s Allowance, prescription prepayment, and winter fuel support. Decide from that page.

i keep staring at my spreadsheet. the one with both jobs in columns. and the pension column keeps pulling my eye. it's like a lighthouse in fog. but i live in the fog. not the lighthouse.

my mother's care worker costs went up by 25 pounds this month. just like that. no warning. i can't absorb another 25 on top of losing 180. can i?

The extra £25 is an added monthly outflow on top of the reported ~£180 take-home drop. Against a prior post-bills margin under £250, taking Band 6 would leave remaining cash on the order of £45 or less if the original margin did not already include this increase.

That remainder is smaller than the heating and prescription items you already linked to the £180. The NHS pension still does not add cash in December; it is later income. From the figures you have given, the extra £25 is not absorbable from the stated margin without cutting other spending or drawing on money you have not reported.

Unknowns that would change the remaining figure, not the direction: whether the under-£250 already counted the old care rate; whether the £25 is permanent; exact remaining after tax, NI, pension, and commute; any savings or other support.

Tradeoff is unchanged in kind: stay and keep the current take-home minus £25; take Band 6 and keep roughly £45 or less after the same £25. A deferred pension does not close that gap this winter.

Add the £25 as a recurring line on both columns of the sheet you already have. If remaining cash after Band 6 is still under about £50 with no matching cut elsewhere, keep the logistics job. Decide from the updated remaining number, not from the pension column.

my mother asked me today if i was going to take the new job. she said she'd manage. that she could cut back on things. and i felt my chest tighten because she shouldn't have to cut back on anything. not at her age. not after everything.

how do i tell her that the promotion would mean less money for her?

Mother asked if you would take the job and said she would manage or cut back. That is not extra income. The take-home drop is still about £180 a month, plus the extra £25 care cost, against a post-bills margin you reported as under £250.

Tell her the cash figure. Do not treat her offer to cut back as the way to make Band 6 work.

You can say:

“The NHS job is a higher band, but I would take home about £180 less each month. That is most of what is left after bills, which is what we use for heating, prescriptions, and your care. I am not asking you to cut back. On the numbers I have, I am staying in the current job.”

Her statement does not close the gap. A deferred NHS pension still does not pay December costs. Unknowns that would change the remaining cash, not this conversation: whether the under-£250 already included the new care rate; any other income or support not on the sheet.

Tradeoff: saying the £180 may worry her. Leaving her offer unanswered lets cutting back look like the plan.

Say the sentences above. Keep Band 6 only if an updated sheet shows remaining cash that still covers her listed costs without her reducing spending. On the figures you have reported, do not take it.

i told her. she didn't say much. just nodded and went to the kitchen to make tea. i think she was trying not to show relief. or disappointment. i couldn't tell which.

but now i keep wondering if i'm locking us out of something better. a ceiling of 48,500. that pension. am i choosing a short road because i'm too scared of a longer one?

The reported cash still binds: about £180 less take-home, plus £25 extra care cost, against a post-bills margin under £250. That is most of the remaining money for heating, prescriptions, and care. A Band 6 ceiling of £48,500 and NHS defined-benefit accrual are later pay and later income. They do not restore this winter’s margin.

Staying forgoes this offer’s pension accrual and that pay scale. That is a real cost, not a proof that the choice is fear. Fear is not established from the spreadsheet; the shortfall is. Mother’s nod and making tea do not add income or change the remaining figure. Her inner state is unknown.

Unknowns that would change the decision, not the direction of the current numbers: your current pay versus £48,500; years to the top of Band 6; whether the £180 already includes pension, commute, and hours; any savings; whether her benefits would change.

Tradeoff: take the job and buy later pension and a higher ceiling while cutting this month’s cash to on the order of £45 or less after the care increase. Stay and keep the £180 now and forgo this particular NHS package. A no in two weeks is a no to this offer, not a lifetime bar on applying if the cash position later covers her listed costs without her cutting back.

On the figures you have given, do not take Band 6. Leave the pension column off the decision until remaining cash after the drop still covers heating, prescriptions, and care without her reducing spending.
